ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *wegaz Proto-West Germanic *weg Old English weġ Old English ealneġ Middle English alwey Proto-Germanic *-as Proto-West Germanic *-as Old English -es Middle English -es Middle English alweyes English always From Middle English alweyes, alwayes, alweys, a variant of Middle English alwey, alway (“always”), from Old English ealneġ, ealne weġ (“always, perpetually”, literally “all the way, all the while, continuously”), from ealne + weġ (accusative case), equivalent to alway + -s.

senses.d: At all times; throughout all time; since the beginning.
ex: Green has always been my favorite color. I’ve loved it for as long as I can remember.

senses.d: Constantly during a certain period, or regularly at stated intervals (opposed to sometimes or occasionally).
ex: In this street, the shops always close during lunchtime.

senses.d: if necessary, or if there is no better option; in any event.
ex: I thought I could always go back to work.
I am her always and she is my always and that’s the whole trouble. For two years I tried to make her pregnant.
What we saw was cute-'n'-cuddly Willow, takin' care of her girl and spouting nauseating platitudes like "You're my always."

ety.text: From Middle French tousjours, from Old French toz jorz, tuzjurz (“without ceasing”, literally “all days”). By surface analysis, tous + jours (compare Dutch altijd (“always”), Danish altid (“always”)). Replaced Old French sempres (“always”), from Latin semper. Cognate with Catalan and Occitan totjorn.
